artiest/frank-boeijen-groep.text:
The Frank Boeijen Groep came from Nijmegen. The singer and guitarist Frank Boeijen first made music in a duo with Wout Pennings. When Pennings left in 1979, Boeijen carried on with a band, which performed for the first time on 3 November 1979 at Doornroosje. The group belongs to the wave of Dutch-language bands that found a large audience after Doe Maar. Where Doe Maar sounded cheerful and familiar, the Frank Boeijen Groep made new wave in their own language, darker and more serious.

The first album, Frank Boeijen Groep (1981), did not reach the chart. The breakthrough came in 1983 with Linda, which reached number 28 in the Top 40. A year later came Zwart wit, which reached number 4. The song is about the murder of fifteen-year-old Kerwin Duinmeijer, who was stabbed to death by a sixteen-year-old skinhead in Amsterdam on the night of 20 to 21 August 1983. After the song Boeijen was given police protection for a time, because the police feared violent reactions. Kronenburg Park (1985), with backing vocals by Mai Tai, reached number 12.

The band's members included the guitarist Will Theunissen and the keyboard player Jos Haagmans. In 1991 Boeijen chose a solo career. The group's last concert was on 30 March 1991 in Almere. Zwart wit shows how the Nederpop of the 1980s also dealt with social issues: racism, violence and a city in which a boy was murdered in the street.
artiest/frank-boeijen-groep.listen: Zwart wit (1984), the example from Mixtapes 7 and 11: notice the cool, clear guitars, which sound like English new wave of those years, and how soberly Boeijen delivers the lyrics about the murder of Kerwin Duinmeijer.

artiest/frank-churchill.text: Frank Churchill (1901–1942) played piano in cinemas and for the radio before he joined Disney in 1930. His song Who's Afraid of the Big Bad Wolf from Three Little Pigs (1933) became a national hit. For Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs (1937), Disney's first feature-length animated film, he wrote songs such as Heigh-Ho and Whistle While You Work with the lyricist Larry Morey. Those songs are not stand-alone numbers but drive the story forward, as later in the Broadway musical. For Dumbo (1941) he won an Oscar with Oliver Wallace. He was still working on Bambi (1942), but died that year.
artiest/frank-churchill.listen: Listen to how the melody stays simple and singable, while the orchestra plays along with small sound effects and the movements of the characters.

artiest/frank-farian.text:
Frank Farian, born Franz Reuther on 18 July 1941 in Kirn, was a German producer and singer. His father was killed in the war before he was born, so his mother brought him up. He first became a cook, then discovered rock 'n' roll, took the name Frank Farian and formed a band. His first single, from 1964, flopped. In 1967 he released a cover of Otis Redding's Mr. Pitiful and then became a familiar name on the German television show Hitparade.

As a singer he scored in 1976 with Rocky, a German-language cover of a song by Austin Roberts, which spent four weeks at number 1 in Germany. His greatest work, however, was done behind the scenes. At the end of 1974 he recorded Baby Do You Wanna Bump under the name Boney M. He then put together a group with the singers Liz Mitchell and Marcia Barrett, the dancer Maizie Williams and the frontman Bobby Farrell. Farrell did not really sing: he moved to Farian's own voice. With Daddy Cool, Rivers of Babylon, Rasputin and Nightflight to Venus, Boney M. became big in Europe and beyond.

That pattern repeated itself later. He also devised the group No Mercy and from 1988 produced Milli Vanilli, whose visible members were not the singers. He also created Far Corporation, with members of Toto, and in 1986 produced Meat Loaf. Farian shows how, in the disco era, the image of a group and the voice on the record could come apart. He died on 23 January 2024.
artiest/frank-farian.listen: Listen to Rocky from 1976 and note that it is a German-language cover of the song by Austin Roberts. Ask yourself what the choice of German does to the sound and feel of the song.

artiest/frank-froeba.text:
Frank Froeba was an American jazz pianist and bandleader. He was born in New Orleans in August 1907 and died in Miami on 16 February 1981. His name is also spelled Froba. As a teenager he was already playing in the bands of Johnny Wiggs and John Tobin. In 1924 and 1925 he worked in New York with Johnny de Droit; after that he led a group of his own in Atlantic City and also played in other dance orchestras.

In 1930 he recorded with Jack Purvis and in 1932 with Jack Bland. From 1933 to 1935 he worked with Benny Goodman. From 1935 until about 1944 he had a band of his own, with which he made recordings for Columbia and Decca. Bunny Berigan, Cozy Cole, Bobby Hackett and Joe Marsala, among others, played in that group. With The Music Goes Round and Round from 1935, and Organ Grinder's Swing and It All Begins and Ends With You, both from 1936, he reached the American charts. In the 1930s and 1940s he was also house pianist for Decca and accompanied Lil Armstrong and Bob Howard, among others.

Froeba is best known as one of the co-writers of Jumpin' Jive, together with Cab Calloway and Jack Palmer. The song became a hit for Calloway and returned in 1981 on Joe Jackson's album Jumpin' Jive. In 1955 Froeba moved to Miami and, under the name Frank Froba, played more popular music. He shows how many pianists in the swing era did their work mainly as accompanists and studio musicians.
artiest/frank-froeba.listen: Listen to Jumpin' Jive, in the version by Cab Calloway or that by Joe Jackson, and notice the swinging, fast-paced vocals and the brass. Try to hear how a song from the 1940s could later be played anew.

artiest/frank-sinatra.text:
Frank Sinatra was born in 1915 in Hoboken, New Jersey, the only child of Italian immigrants. As a boy he listened to big bands and admired Bing Crosby. He never learned to read music; he learned everything by ear. In 1935 he won a radio talent contest with the vocal group the Hoboken Four. In 1939 he became a singer in Harry James's band, then in Tommy Dorsey's orchestra. In the early 1940s he became the idol of the bobby soxers, teenage girls who formed a whole new audience for popular music.

In the early 1950s his popularity slumped, but in 1953 he won an Oscar for his role in the film From Here to Eternity. At Capitol Records he then made his most admired albums with the arranger Nelson Riddle, such as In the Wee Small Hours (1955) and Songs for Swingin' Lovers! (1956). In 1960 he started his own label, Reprise. He recorded with Count Basie, Antonio Carlos Jobim and Duke Ellington. In 1971 he stopped for a while, after releasing My Way, but two years later he was back. In 1980 New York, New York came out.

Sinatra began in the swing era and remained a singer of the great orchestras all his life. His voice was called powerful and charismatic, but also tender, and he was nicknamed The Voice. He was one of the first teen idols of popular music. The critic Robert Christgau called him the greatest singer of the twentieth century. He was also a successful film actor. He died in 1998.
artiest/frank-sinatra.listen: Listen to a track from In the Wee Small Hours, with arrangements by Nelson Riddle. Notice how clearly Sinatra pronounces every word and how the orchestra frames his voice without drowning it out.

artiest/frank-strobel.text:
Frank Strobel is a German conductor, born in 1966 in Munich. He grew up in his parents' cinema, taught himself to be a projectionist and so came into contact with film and film music at a young age. Later he became a musician and conductor. Until 1998 he was principal conductor of the Deutsches Filmorchester Babelsberg. Since 2000 he has led the European Film Philharmonic and advised on the silent film programming of ZDF and Arte.

Strobel became known for his work on film in the concert hall. He is the recognised editor of music by Alfred Schnittke and from 2001 contributed to Schnittke's reputation as a film composer in the German-speaking world. With the Rundfunk-Sinfonieorchester Berlin he recorded several pieces by Schnittke, including the series Film Music. In 2003 and 2004 he had success in Berlin and Moscow with a concert accompanying the film Alexander Nevsky with music by Prokofiev, for which he reconstructed the original score. In November 2004 he received the highest Russian civilian honour at the Bolshoi Theatre in Moscow. On 12 February 2012 he conducted the world premiere of the reconstructed version of Metropolis, performed by the Rundfunk-Sinfonieorchester Berlin.

Strobel has provided music for more than forty silent films, often in performances that were broadcast on television. He is among the pioneers of the film-in-concert movement, in which an orchestra plays the music to a film live. In doing so he has brought film music out of the shadow of the image.
artiest/frank-strobel.listen: Listen to a piece from Schnittke's Film Music in Strobel's recordings and notice how the music tells a story of its own even without the picture. Ask yourself which scene you would expect to go with it.

artiest/frank-wilson.text:
Frank Edward Wilson was an American songwriter, singer and producer for Motown Records. He was born on 5 December 1940 in Houston, Texas, and died on 27 September 2012. He studied for a year at Southern University in Baton Rouge, but lost his scholarship after a civil rights protest. As a teenager he moved to Los Angeles. In 1963 Berry Gordy asked the producers Hal Davis and Marc Gordon to open a Motown office in Los Angeles, and Wilson joined that team. The first single to appear from that West Coast branch, Stevie by Patrice Holloway in December 1963, also carried his name as a writer.

Wilson also started publishing companies of his own and, over four years, wrote and produced more than forty compositions for others. He also recorded a single himself, Do I Love You (Indeed I Do), which was to appear as a Motown release on the Soul label. Reportedly 250 demo copies were pressed, but Wilson preferred to concentrate on producing and had them destroyed. In 1976 he left Motown, became a born-again Christian and a minister, and wrote books with his wife Bunny.

Do I Love You (Indeed I Do) from 1965 is a soul song with the typical Motown build: a solid rhythm section, tambourine and a singer who sings with great power. The story of the almost vanished record shows how chancy it is that a classic comes into being, and that it is sometimes the makers behind the scenes who write soul history.
artiest/frank-wilson.listen: Listen to Do I Love You (Indeed I Do) and notice the rhythm of the band and Wilson's voice. Can you hear how the singer almost shouts above the band and how the accompaniment keeps driving him on?

artiest/frank-wright.text:
Frank Wright was an American free jazz saxophonist, born in 1935 in Grenada, Mississippi. He grew up in Memphis and Cleveland and began as a bass guitarist in rhythm and blues bands. In that capacity he accompanied Bobby Bland and B.B. King, among others. In Cleveland he met Albert Ayler, and afterwards he switched to the tenor saxophone. In 1964 he moved to New York, where he played with Sunny Murray and Noah Howard and played with John Coltrane.

At the end of 1965 he recorded his first album for the small label ESP-Disk, Frank Wright Trio, with Henry Grimes on bass and Tom Price on drums. In 1967 came Your Prayer. His playing was wild and fierce: he made the saxophone scream, honk and crack. Critics often compared him with Ayler, but Wright also kept hearing the earthy funk of R&B and gospel. His music was sometimes called energy music in the 1960s. At times he became so caught up in his playing that he began to dance in the middle of a solo.

In 1969 Wright moved to Paris, where for years he led a quartet with Bobby Few and Alan Silva, among others. Later he played in Cecil Taylor's orchestra. Colleagues called him the Reverend, because of his spiritual approach to music. He never made a record for a major label and remained in the underground throughout his career. He died in Germany in 1990.
artiest/frank-wright.listen: Listen to The Earth and pay attention only to the sound of the saxophone: how Wright makes the tone scream and crack over. Do not look for a melody you can sing along to, but for the energy and colour of the sound.

artiest/frank-zappa.text:
Frank Zappa was born on 21 December 1940 in Baltimore and grew up in California. As a teenager he listened at the same time to Black rhythm and blues, doo-wop and modern composers such as Igor Stravinsky and Edgard Varèse. He first played drums in R&B bands and later switched to the electric guitar, while already writing classical pieces at school.

With his band The Mothers of Invention he made his debut in 1966 with Freak Out!, an album that alternated mocking, seemingly ordinary rock 'n' roll songs with long sound collages. He kept up that idiosyncratic approach for more than thirty years. He released more than sixty albums, including Hot Rats (1969), Apostrophe (’) (1974) and Joe’s Garage (1979), and produced almost all of them himself. He wrote rock, jazz, jazz rock and orchestral works, directed films and designed album covers.

His music is full of changes of time signature, improvisation and sound experiments, and his lyrics poke fun at American society. Recurring melodies, ideas and characters link his albums to one another. Zappa fought against censorship and was critical of education and organised religion. Unlike many of his contemporaries he rejected drug use. In Europe he had more success than in his own country. He died on 4 December 1993 and was inducted posthumously into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1995. He is regarded as one of the most innovative and versatile musicians of the twentieth century.
artiest/frank-zappa.listen: Listen to The Return of the Son of Monster Magnet, the long closing piece of Freak Out! (1966). Notice how there is hardly a song left: voices, percussion and sound effects together form a collage.

artiest/frankie-goes-to-hollywood.text:
Frankie Goes to Hollywood originated in 1980 in Liverpool around the singer Holly Johnson. The name came from an announcement of Frank Sinatra's first film. In 1982 Johnson started again with the drummer Peter Gill and the bassist Mark O'Toole. The guitarist Brian Nash and the dancer and backing singer Paul Rutherford completed the group. Johnson wanted a provocative, modern band that brought punk and disco together.

In 1983 the group became the first act on ZTT, producer Trevor Horn's new label. The first single, Relax, became an enormous hit after the BBC banned it because of its sexual lyrics. After that Two Tribes, about the threat of nuclear war, and The Power of Love also went to number 1 in England. The debut album Welcome to the Pleasuredome (1984) had more than a million advance orders before its release. According to one music journalist, no band dominated a year the way Frankie dominated 1984. The second album, Liverpool (1986), sold less, and in 1987 the group fell apart in quarrels.

Johnson and Rutherford were among the first openly gay pop singers, and the band made sexuality and gay rights a subject of its music and performances. Trevor Horn's big, glossy production, full of synthesizers and electronic rhythms, was at least as important as the band itself. In this way Frankie Goes to Hollywood became one of the clearest examples of the studio pop of the 1980s.
artiest/frankie-goes-to-hollywood.listen: Listen to Relax (1983). Notice the thudding electronic bass line and Trevor Horn's inflated production, and how Holly Johnson's voice cuts straight through it.

artiest/frankie-knuckles.text:
Frankie Knuckles was born in 1955 in the Bronx in New York as Francis Warren Nicholls Jr. As a teenager he went to discos with his friend Larry Levan, and later they DJed together. In 1977 he moved to Chicago to become resident DJ at The Warehouse, a club with mainly Black and gay patrons. House music is named after that club, and Knuckles was often called the godfather of house music.

At The Warehouse Knuckles played disco, soul and European synth-pop. In the late 1970s he began to edit records himself: he lengthened intros and breaks and put extra beats under them. He also played tapes on a reel-to-reel recorder, and in 1983 he bought his first drum machine. At the end of 1982 he started his own club, The Power Plant. Your Love was written by the Chicago singer Jamie Principle, whose own version appeared in 1986. In 1987 the label Trax released a version credited to Knuckles. Both versions open with a synthesizer arpeggio, followed by a bass line.

In the 1990s Knuckles became a much-in-demand remixer. The Whistle Song (1991) from his debut album Beyond the Mix became his first number 1 on the American dance chart. In 1998 he won the Grammy for remixer of the year. Since 2004 a stretch of Jefferson Street in Chicago has been called Frankie Knuckles Way. He died in 2014 in Chicago. The British group The Source mixed Your Love in 1991 with the vocals of Candi Staton into the hit You Got the Love.
artiest/frankie-knuckles.listen: Your Love (1987): notice the synthesizer arpeggio with which the track opens and which keeps running, even when the bass line and Jamie Principle's vocals come in. That repetition keeps the dance floor moving.

artiest/frankie-laine.text:
Frankie Laine, born Francesco Paolo LoVecchio, was an American singer and songwriter. He was born on 30 March 1913 in Chicago, to a family that had emigrated from Monreale in Sicily. As a boy he sang in his school choir, and he decided to become a singer after seeing Al Jolson in The Singing Fool. His career spanned almost seventy-five years: from his first performances in 1930 with a dance marathon company to his last performance of That's My Desire in 2005. He died on 6 February 2007.

Laine was billed as America's Number One Song Stylist and had nicknames such as Mr. Rhythm and Old Leather Lungs. His hits included That's My Desire, That Lucky Old Sun, Mule Train, Jezebel, High Noon, I Believe, Cool Water and Rawhide. He sang the title songs of westerns such as 3:10 to Yuma, Gunfight at the O.K. Corral and Blazing Saddles. High Noon was sung in the film by Tex Ritter, but Laine's own version, with slightly altered lyrics, became a bigger hit. He did not sing the theme of Champion the Wonder Horse in the series either, but his own recording became better known.

Laine sang in a wide range of styles, from big band crooning to pop, gospel, rock, folk, jazz and blues. He belonged to the great singers of the pre-rock 'n' roll era and showed that a voice with power and breath control could take on an entire orchestra. His lasting popularity was shown in 2011, when a compilation of his hits reached number 16 on the British album chart.
artiest/frankie-laine.listen: Listen to Rawhide and notice the power and breath control of his voice. Observe how the singing sounds almost like a command, fitting the western theme.

artiest/frankie-trumbauer.text:
Frankie Trumbauer, in full Orie Frank Trumbauer, was an American jazz saxophonist of the 1920s and 1930s. He was born on 30 May 1901 in Carbondale, Illinois, grew up in St. Louis and died on 11 June 1956. His main instrument was the C-melody saxophone, an instrument that is rare today and falls between alto and tenor in size and pitch. He also played alto saxophone, bassoon and clarinet. His first important work was done in the orchestras of Edgar Benson and Ray Miller and with the Mound City Blue Blowers.

Trumbauer brought Bix Beiderbecke into Jean Goldkette's orchestra, of which he became musical director. In 1927 he moved with Beiderbecke to Paul Whiteman, with whom he played for eight of the next nine years. That year he also signed with Okeh and recorded Singin' the Blues, with Beiderbecke on cornet and Eddie Lang on guitar. That recording became a hit and entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1977. Other well-known titles were Krazy Kat, Trumbology and For No Reason at All in C. In 1931 he made the first hit version of Georgia on My Mind.

Trumbauer is regarded as one of the most influential saxophonists of his time. Lester Young called him his idol and tried to get the sound of a C-melody on the tenor saxophone. His partnership with Beiderbecke produced some of the best jazz records of the late 1920s. In 2001 Ken Burns used a photograph of him with his saxophone as a symbol for jazz in the documentary Jazz.
artiest/frankie-trumbauer.listen: Listen to Singin' the Blues from 1927 and notice Trumbauer's relaxed, light solo on the C-melody saxophone. Then try to recognise the reply from Bix Beiderbecke's cornet.

artiest/franz-lehar.text:
Franz Lehár was an Austro-Hungarian composer, born on 30 April 1870 in Komárom, now Komárno in Slovakia, and died on 24 October 1948. His father was a bandmaster in an army regiment, and his mother came from a Hungarian family of German descent. Franz studied violin at the Prague Conservatory. Antonín Dvořák advised him to concentrate on composition. He wrote sonatas, symphonic poems and marches, but became famous mainly for his operettas.

The best-known and most successful work is Die lustige Witwe from 1905, which in English is called The Merry Widow. He also wrote Der Graf von Luxemburg, Zigeunerliebe from 1910, Das Land des Lächelns, Der Zarewitsch and Giuditta, among others. He also composed waltzes, of which Gold und Silber is the most popular. The tenor Richard Tauber sang in many of his operettas, from a revival of Zigeunerliebe in 1920 and in Frasquita in 1922.

Lehár wrote melodic, elegant music for orchestra and singers, full of waltz rhythms and songs that stay in the mind. The Vilja-Lied from Die lustige Witwe is a well-known example. With his operettas he took the light theatre of Vienna out into the world and wrote pieces that are still performed today. He belongs to the roots of popular music in the theatre, where the song is central.
artiest/franz-lehar.listen: Listen to the Vilja-Lied from Die lustige Witwe and follow the soprano line: notice how the melody begins softly and rises in waves, while the orchestra mainly supports the beat and the mood.

artiest/franz-liszt.text: Franz Liszt was the greatest piano virtuoso of his time and caused a veritable Lisztomania on his tours. He was one of the first to play an entire concert on his own, and he pushed back the boundaries of what a pianist can do. From 1848 he worked as Kapellmeister in Weimar, where he developed the symphonic poem and defended the music of Wagner. His Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2 moves from a sombre, free opening to a whirling dance.
artiest/franz-liszt.listen: Listen to Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2 and hear how heavy, free chords sound like a Gypsy orchestra slowly warming up.

artiest/franz-schubert.text: Franz Schubert lived in Vienna almost all his life and had few public successes, but his music was heard at evenings with friends, the Schubertiads. He wrote more than six hundred songs and made the song for voice and piano a fully fledged art form. In Erlkönig from 1815 the piano plays the galloping horse, while a single singer portrays the narrator, the father, the child and the Erlking. He died in 1828, only thirty-one years old.
artiest/franz-schubert.listen: Listen to the beginning of Erlkönig and hear how the lightning-fast repeated notes in the piano make the horse gallop through the night.

artiest/franz-schubert-dietrich-fischer-.text:
This entry is about two people who come together in one recording. Franz Schubert was a Viennese composer of the early nineteenth century. He died young, in 1828, and in a short time wrote more than six hundred songs for voice and piano. His Ständchen, D. 889, from 1828, is a setting of Horch, horch, die Lerch, a poem from Shakespeare's play in German translation. It is a serenade: a song that a lover sings at a window.

Dietrich Fischer-Dieskau was a German lyric baritone and conductor, born on 28 May 1925 in Berlin and died on 18 May 2012. After the war he became one of the most famous performers of the Lied, the German art song. He sang in public for the first time in 1947, made his debut in 1948 at the Städtische Oper in Berlin and, together with sopranos such as Elisabeth Schwarzkopf and Irmgard Seefried, recorded albums of songs by Schubert and Hugo Wolf. He is best known for his interpretation of Schubert's Winterreise.

In such a recording you hear how a singer tells a whole story with only voice and piano. The music is simple in design: a melody, an accompaniment and a text that is the heart of the song. The course uses this piece to show how far the art of song goes back before popular music existed, and how important the voice as instrument and storyteller already was.
artiest/franz-schubert-dietrich-fischer-.listen: Listen to Ständchen and notice how the singer delivers the words of the text, softly and with great nuance. Can you hear how the piano gives the serenade a rocking movement of its own?

artiest/franz-von-suppe.text:
Franz von Suppé was an Austrian composer of light operas and other theatre music. He was born on 18 April 1819 in Spalato, present-day Split in Croatia, and grew up in Zara, present-day Zadar. His mother tongue was Italian. After his father's death in 1835 the family moved to Vienna, where he was taught by Ignaz von Seyfried, a pupil of Mozart. He played flute in orchestras, gave Italian lessons and from 1840 worked as a composer and conductor for theatres in Vienna and the surrounding area. He died on 21 May 1895 in Vienna.

Suppé wrote about thirty operettas and a hundred and eighty farces, ballets and other stage works. He also wrote a great deal of church music, including a Requiem for Franz Pokorny from 1855 and the Missa Dalmatica. Most of the operettas are forgotten, with a few exceptions: Boccaccio, Die schöne Galathée and Fatinitza. His name lives on in his overtures, such as Dichter und Bauer, Leichte Kavallerie, Ein Morgen, ein Mittag und ein Abend in Wien and Pique Dame. Many conductors have recorded them, including Karajan, Solti and Mehta.

According to the musicologist Robert Letellier, Suppé mastered three styles: Italian opera buffa, French opéra-comique and German. He blended them with experience as a theatre conductor and a solid classical technique. His overtures are a large part of the reason why Viennese operetta remained so well known outside the theatre too.
artiest/franz-von-suppe.listen: Listen to the overture to Leichte Kavallerie and notice the trumpet calls and the galloping rhythms. Try to hear how an overture can work like a short opera without singers.

artiest/franz-waxman.text: Franz Waxman was born in 1906 in Königshütte, Germany, and worked in Berlin as a pianist and arranger for jazz bands and cabaret. After being attacked by Nazis in 1934, he left via Paris for Hollywood. His first big score, Bride of Frankenstein (1935), combines humour and horror with colourful orchestration. Waxman worked a great deal with Alfred Hitchcock, on Rebecca (1940) and Rear Window (1954), among others. He used jazz early on as a serious tone colour in film music. For Sunset Boulevard (1950) and A Place in the Sun (1951) he won an Oscar in two consecutive years. In 1947 he founded a music festival of his own in Los Angeles, where he conducted new concert music.
artiest/franz-waxman.listen: Notice the colourful orchestration: unusual combinations of instruments and soft jazz sounds alongside a classical orchestra.

artiest/fred-astaire.text:
Fred Astaire was born Frederick Austerlitz on 10 May 1899 in Omaha, Nebraska, and died on 22 June 1987. He was a dancer, actor, singer, musician and choreographer, with a career on stage, film and television that lasted seventy-six years. His mother wanted to escape from Omaha with her children's talents. In 1905 the family moved to New York, where Fred and his sister Adele trained in dance. On their mother's advice they changed their name to Astaire.

In Hollywood he appeared in ten musicals with Ginger Rogers, including Top Hat from 1935, Swing Time from 1936 and Shall We Dance from 1937. Later came films such as Holiday Inn in 1942 and Easter Parade in 1948. In 1950 he received an Academy Honorary Award and in 1978 the Kennedy Center Honors. Night and Day from 1932, a song by Cole Porter, belongs to his early work. He also sang on records, such as The Astaire Story from 1953.

Astaire drew on tap dance, classical ballet and the refined style of Vernon and Irene Castle, and himself called his approach the outlaw style. His style had a great influence on American Smooth, a form of ballroom dance. As a singer he had a light, natural voice, and many composers wrote songs for him. He was regarded as the greatest popular dancer of all time and showed how dance and song in film together tell a story.
artiest/fred-astaire.listen: Listen to Night and Day and notice how lightly and effortlessly Astaire sings the melody, almost like spoken text. Can you hear how the rhythm of the accompaniment recalls his dancing?

artiest/fred-van-hove.text:
Fred Van Hove was a Belgian jazz musician and a pioneer of European free jazz. He was born on 19 February 1937 in Antwerp and died on 13 January 2022. He was a pianist, accordionist, church organist, carillonneur and composer, and worked mainly with improvisation. At first it did not look as if he would end up in jazz: he took twelve years of classical lessons at the Merksem Music Academy in theory, harmony and piano. A performance in 1960 at the Lazy River Jazz Festival in Kortrijk nevertheless led him to jazz, and he played in Mike Zinzen's ensemble.

From 1966 he played in the quartets and sextets of the saxophonist Peter Brötzmann, including on Machine Gun from 1968. After that he formed a trio with Brötzmann and the Dutch drummer Han Bennink. In Antwerp he founded the WIM Bigband, WIM standing for Werkgroep Improviserende Musici (Working Group of Improvising Musicians), and later Musica Libera Antverpiae and the Pistri Ensemble. On albums such as Balls from 1970 and Tschüs from 1975 he presented his own work, and he also became known as a soloist. He also played in duos with Steve Lacy, Lol Coxhill, Albert Mangelsdorff and Vinko Globokar, among others.

Van Hove wrote music for film and theatre, taught in Berlin and gave workshops in Germany, France, England, Belgium and the Netherlands. In 1996 the Flemish government appointed him Cultural Ambassador of Flanders. He shows that European free jazz had a scene of its own, independent of the American examples.
artiest/fred-van-hove.listen: Listen to a recording of the trio with Peter Brötzmann and Han Bennink and notice how Van Hove's piano often works as a second rhythm instrument. Try to hear who leads the conversation.

artiest/freddie-green.text:
Freddie Green, in full Frederick William Green, was an American swing guitarist who played rhythm guitar for almost fifty years in Count Basie's orchestra. He was born on 31 March 1911 in Charleston, South Carolina, and died on 1 March 1987. He first learned banjo and took up the guitar as a young teenager. A friend of his father's, Sam Walker, taught him to read music and arranged his first performance in a local group, in which the later trumpeter Cat Anderson also played. After the death of his parents he went to New York, where he played in clubs as a teenager.

The talent scout John Hammond heard him there and introduced him to Basie. In 1937 Basie visited a performance by Green with his orchestra and offered him work on the spot. Apart from a brief interruption, Green remained a fixture in the band for the next fifty years. He himself made only a few records under his own name, such as Mr. Rhythm from 1956 and Swing Reunion from 1985.

Green's role was to accompany, and he rarely played solo. He changed chords often, sometimes on every beat, and used his left hand to mute the strings that were not meant to sound. He said that you should never hear the guitar separately, but as part of the drums, as if the drummer were playing chords. In this way he helped to establish rhythm guitar as a regular part of the rhythm section of a big band. His even, beat-counting playing is an important part of the sound associated with Basie.
artiest/freddie-green.listen: Listen to a recording by the Count Basie Orchestra from the 1940s or 1950s and notice the guitar playing on every beat. You rarely hear Green separately, but you would notice the swing if he were to stop.

artiest/freddie-hubbard.text:
Freddie Hubbard was an American jazz trumpeter, born in 1938 in Indianapolis. In the school band he tried all kinds of brass instruments, but the trumpet became his main instrument. As a teenager he was already playing with the brothers Wes and Monk Montgomery. In 1958 he moved to New York, where he was soon playing with Sonny Rollins, Eric Dolphy and Quincy Jones. In 1960 he made his first album of his own for Blue Note, Open Sesame.

In 1961 he took Lee Morgan's place in drummer Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers. There he played alongside Wayne Shorter, on albums such as Mosaic and Free for All. Hubbard had a powerful, clear tone and a blistering technique, and played mainly hard bop. Yet he had one foot in free jazz: he played on Ornette Coleman's Free Jazz and on John Coltrane's Ascension. He could also be heard on classics such as Herbie Hancock's Maiden Voyage and Shorter's Speak No Evil. In the 1960s he recorded eight albums under his own name for Blue Note.

In the 1970s he had his greatest success at the label CTI, with Red Clay (1970) and First Light (1971), which won a Grammy. Later he played with Hancock, Shorter, Ron Carter and Tony Williams in the group V.S.O.P. Hubbard died in 2008. His recognisable tone gave modern jazz new directions.
artiest/freddie-hubbard.listen: Listen to Arietis and notice Hubbard's trumpet: how fast and clear he plays, and how his solo grows steadily higher and fiercer. Hear too how the rhythm section holds the tempo tight.

artiest/freddie-king.text:
Freddie King, also spelled Freddy King, was an American blues guitarist, singer and songwriter. He was born on 3 September 1934 in Gilmer, Texas, and died on 28 December 1976. His mother and an uncle taught him to play guitar at the age of six. In 1949 the family moved from Dallas to the South Side of Chicago. There, as a teenager, he sneaked into the clubs and heard Muddy Waters, Howlin' Wolf, T-Bone Walker and Elmore James. His first band was called the Every Hour Blues Boys, and by day he worked in a steel mill.

After rejections from Chess Records, King signed with Federal Records. His breakthrough came in 1961 with the single Have You Ever Loved a Woman and the instrumental Hide Away, which reached number five on Billboard's R&B chart in 1961. Hide Away became a blues standard. The album Freddy King Sings from 1961 showcased his singing and contains I'm Tore Down, among others. Later he worked with producers who leaned more towards rhythm and blues and rock, and he was one of the first blues musicians to have a mixed band on stage.

King's style derives from Texas and Chicago blues. Together with Albert King and B.B. King he is regarded as one of the Three Kings of the Blues Guitar, although they were not related. He had a great influence on electric blues and on later guitarists. In 2012 ZZ Top inducted him into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, and Hide Away is on the list of 500 Songs that Shaped Rock.
artiest/freddie-king.listen: Listen to Hide Away and notice how the guitar carries the melody without vocals. Try to hear how the guitar takes the place of the singer.

artiest/freddie-mercury.text:
Freddie Mercury's real name was Farrokh Bulsara. He was born in 1946 in Stone Town on Zanzibar, the child of Indian parents from the Parsi community. From the age of eight he attended a British boarding school in India. There he had piano lessons, began calling himself Freddie and played songs by Cliff Richard, Elvis Presley and Little Richard in a school band. In 1964 the family fled the revolution on Zanzibar for England. Mercury studied graphic design at Ealing art college and played in a series of bands.

In 1970 he became the singer of Smile, the band of the guitarist Brian May and the drummer Roger Taylor. In 1971 the bassist John Deacon joined, and Mercury chose the new name: Queen. He also designed the band's logo. For Queen he wrote hits such as Killer Queen, Bohemian Rhapsody, Somebody to Love, We Are the Champions, Don't Stop Me Now and Crazy Little Thing Called Love. He also made solo records, such as Mr. Bad Guy (1985) and Barcelona (1988) with the Spanish soprano Montserrat Caballé.

Mercury had a vocal range of four octaves and could move within a few bars from a raw rock voice to a clear, high tenor. He broke with the image of the tough rock singer through his theatrical style, which also determined Queen's direction. On stage he drew the audience into his performance, as at Live Aid in 1985. In 1987 he was diagnosed with AIDS. He died in 1991, a day after making his illness public. In 1992 a concert was held for him at Wembley Stadium, in aid of the fight against AIDS.
artiest/freddie-mercury.listen: Listen to Bohemian Rhapsody and follow Mercury's voice through the song. Hear how the song begins as a ballad at the piano, moves into an operatic section with stacked voices and then erupts into hard rock.

artiest/freddy-quinn.text:
Freddy Quinn, born Franz Eugen Helmut Manfred Nidl on 27 September 1931 in Niederfladnitz in Lower Austria, is an Austrian singer and actor who became hugely popular in the German-speaking world in the late 1950s and the 1960s. He grew up in Vienna. There are stories about his youth that are not all certain, but what is certain is that he was discovered in Hamburg, in the St. Pauli district, and received his first record contract in 1954.

In 1956 Quinn sang for Germany at the Eurovision Song Contest in Lugano, with So geht das jede Nacht. He did not win, but Heimweh from the same year was a great success. Hits followed such as Die Gitarre und das Meer and Unter fremden Sternen in 1959, Irgendwann gibt's ein Wiedersehn in 1960, La Paloma in 1961 and Junge, komm bald wieder in 1962. Vergangen, vergessen, vorüber from 1964 was another million-seller. He also appeared in films, such as Freddy, die Gitarre und das Meer from 1959 and Heimweh nach St. Pauli from 1963.

Quinn took over the image of the restless wanderer who sails the seas but longs for home, as Hans Albers had two generations earlier. His songs are schlagers with guitar and a soft, warm voice, full of homesickness and longing. In this way he became one of the faces of the German schlager in the years of the postwar miracle, when many people recognised their own longing for home in his.
artiest/freddy-quinn.listen: Listen to Heimweh and notice how the singer evokes longing with a soft, somewhat sombre voice, accompanied by guitar and orchestra. Which word or which key gives the song that homesick atmosphere?

artiest/frederic-chopin.text: Frédéric Chopin grew up in Warsaw and from 1831 lived in Paris, where he preferred to play in salons rather than in large halls. He wrote almost exclusively for piano and gave the instrument a singing tone, with melodies that are ornamented the way an opera singer would do it. His Nocturne Op. 9 No. 2, published in 1832, is the best-known example. With his mazurkas and polonaises he brought the dances of Poland into the concert hall.
artiest/frederic-chopin.listen: Listen to the Nocturne and hear how the right hand plays a singing melody that is more richly ornamented at each repeat, above a calmly rocking accompaniment.

artiest/frederic-devreese.text: Frédéric Devreese was a Belgian composer and conductor, son of the composer Godfried Devreese. He studied in Mechelen, Brussels and Rome and worked for a long time at the Belgian broadcasting organisation. His most important film work was done for the director André Delvaux, the founder of Belgian magical realism. That began with De man die zijn haar kort liet knippen (1966) and continued with Un soir, un train (1968), Benvenuta (1983) and L'oeuvre au noir (1988). Devreese wrote lyrical, tonal orchestral music with dance forms such as the waltz, tango and habanera. His music helps to create Delvaux's dreamlike atmosphere, in which reality and imagination run into one another.
artiest/frederic-devreese.listen: Notice the dance rhythms, such as tango and waltz, and the melancholy melody that hovers between dream and reality.

artiest/free.text:
Free was an English rock band, formed in London in 1968 by the singer and guitarist Paul Rodgers, the guitarist Paul Kossoff, the bassist and keyboard player Andy Fraser and the drummer Simon Kirke. Kossoff and Kirke knew each other from Black Cat Bones. Kossoff heard Rodgers in an R&B club in Finsbury Park and asked if he could play along. Alexis Korner recommended Fraser and came up with the name Free. The first gig was on 19 April 1968 in Battersea. The band members were teenagers: Fraser was fifteen, Kossoff seventeen, Rodgers and Kirke eighteen.

In November 1968 they recorded their first album, Tons of Sobs, which was released on Island Records in March 1969. Free followed that same year. Both records sold modestly, although the band was known for its live performances and ceaseless touring. The breakthrough came with Fire and Water in 1970, with the hit All Right Now. As a result the group was invited to play at the Isle of Wight Festival in 1970, before an audience of 600,000 people. Highway followed in 1970 and Free at Last in 1972. Fraser left in 1972, and after Heartbreaker in 1973 the band broke up.

Rodgers and Kirke then formed Bad Company, Kossoff Back Street Crawler. Kossoff died in 1976 at the age of twenty-five. Free played blues rock and was famous for its live shows. Rolling Stone called the band pioneers of British hard rock. All Right Now remains a fixture on the radio.
artiest/free.listen: Listen to All Right Now and notice Paul Rodgers's vocals and Paul Kossoff's guitar. Try to hear how four people together make such a full sound.

artiest/frenna.text:
Frenna, real name Francis Edusei, is a Dutch rapper and singer, born on 17 November 1991 in The Hague. His family comes from Ghana. Rap was at first a hobby. Together with three friends he formed the group Strictly Family Business, SFB for short. They often practised by rapping in the car about whatever came into their heads. Their first recording was based on Zieknieh, which they played at a friend's birthday party. Its success led to Flexen, the group's debut single, which became a club hit.

Frenna then seriously chose to make music his career. For the album New Wave from 2015 he received, with other rappers, the Pop Prize (Popprijs) at Noorderslag. His solo albums are Geen oog dichtgedaan from 2016, Francis from 2018, Championships and Highest from 2021 and Pink Summer from 2024. In 2018 he broke the Dutch Spotify record for the most streams in one day after release with Verleden Tijd, and the song spent six weeks at the top of the Dutch Top 40. In February 2019 he received an Edison Pop Award for Francis for the first time. At the end of 2019 he was the most-streamed Dutch artist on Spotify.

Frenna raps and sings, and the choruses of his songs often arise from a freestyle. With Highest he also tried to win more listeners internationally. He belongs to the group of Dutch artists who used streaming platforms in the 2010s to reach large audiences.
artiest/frenna.listen: Listen to Verleden Tijd and notice the difference between the verses and the chorus. Can you hear where the rapping turns into singing?

artiest/friedrich-cerha.text:
Friedrich Cerha was an Austrian composer, conductor and teacher. He was born on 17 February 1926 in Vienna and died there on 14 February 2023. He played violin at the age of six and began composing two years later. In 1943 he was called up for the army, and he deserted twice. After the war he studied at the Vienna music academy and in 1950 took a doctorate in German studies. From 1950 to 1962 he was a teacher of music and German, and he continued to perform as a violinist.

From 1956 Cerha attended the Darmstadt Summer Courses, where he felt that a new era was beginning. In 1958, with Kurt Schwertsik, he founded the ensemble die reihe, which played a large part in spreading new music in Austria. His work Relazioni fragili was heard in 1958 in Darmstadt and in 1961 at the ISCM festival in Vienna. He was also known as an interpreter of Alban Berg, Arnold Schoenberg and Anton Webern. In 1962 he began work on the unfinished third act of Berg's opera Lulu. Pierre Boulez conducted the complete opera in Paris in 1979.

Cerha's own operas include Baal after Brecht, performed in Salzburg in 1981, Der Rattenfänger and Der Riese vom Steinfeld, in Vienna in 2002. His cycle Spiegel, begun in 1960, is regarded as one of his core works. From 1976 to 1988 he was professor of composition in Vienna, with students such as Georg Friedrich Haas and Karlheinz Essl. He received the Ernst von Siemens Music Prize in 2012, among other honours. His importance lies in the Viennese tradition of Berg, which he kept alive thanks to his completion of Lulu.
artiest/friedrich-cerha.listen: Listen to an excerpt from Spiegel and notice how the music develops. Do you hear a melody, or rather a sound that slowly changes?

artiest/friedrich-hollaender.text:
Friedrich Hollaender, in exile also Frederick Hollander, was a German film composer and writer. He was born on 18 October 1896 in London, into a Jewish family. His father, the operetta composer Victor Hollaender, was musical director of the Barnum & Bailey circus there. In 1899 the family returned to Berlin. Hollaender studied at the Stern Conservatory in the master class of Engelbert Humperdinck and in the evenings played piano for silent films, which taught him to improvise. He died on 18 January 1976.

After his studies he wrote music for productions by Max Reinhardt and became a fixture of the Berlin cabaret world, together with Kurt Tucholsky, Klabund, Walter Mehring and Mischa Spoliansky. In 1931 he founded the cabaret Tingel-Tangel-Theater. His breakthrough came with the film music for Der Blaue Engel in 1930, with the song Ich bin von Kopf bis Fuß auf Liebe eingestellt, known in English as Falling in Love Again (Can't Help It), sung by Marlene Dietrich.

Because of his Jewish background he had to leave Germany in 1933. He went first to Paris and in 1934 emigrated to the United States. There he wrote music for more than a hundred films, including Destry Rides Again, A Foreign Affair, The 5,000 Fingers of Dr. T. and Sabrina, and received four Oscar nominations. Many of his songs became famous anew through Marlene Dietrich. In A Foreign Affair he can be seen himself as a pianist. Hollaender links the Berlin cabaret of the 1920s to the Hollywood film.
artiest/friedrich-hollaender.listen: Listen to Falling in Love Again (Can't Help It) in Marlene Dietrich's performance and notice her low, almost spoken style of singing. The song comes from Der Blaue Engel from 1930.

artiest/fritz-reiner.text:
Fritz Reiner, in Hungarian Reiner Frigyes, was a Hungarian-American conductor of opera and symphonic music. He was born on 19 December 1888 in Budapest into a non-religious Jewish family. At his father's insistence he began to study law, but he chose piano and composition at the Franz Liszt Academy after all. One of his piano teachers was Béla Bartók. He then conducted at the opera houses of Budapest and Dresden, where he worked closely with Richard Strauss.

In 1922 he moved to the United States, where he was conductor of the Cincinnati Symphony Orchestra until 1931. He then taught at the Curtis Institute in Philadelphia, where Leonard Bernstein, Lukas Foss and Nino Rota were among his students. From 1938 to 1948 he led the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra. In 1949 he conducted Strauss's Salome at the Metropolitan Opera, and in 1951 the American premiere of Stravinsky's The Rake's Progress. From 1953 until his death in 1963 he was principal conductor of the Chicago Symphony Orchestra. With that orchestra he made stereo recordings for RCA as early as 1954.

Reiner was known for precision and economical gestures. Stravinsky called the Chicago orchestra under his direction the most precise and flexible in the world, but his way of working was autocratic and sometimes hard on the musicians. Together with Joseph Szigeti he persuaded Serge Koussevitzky to have Bartók write the Concerto for Orchestra. He was an authority on the music of Strauss, Bartók and Stravinsky and championed new music. He died on 15 November 1963 in New York.
artiest/fritz-reiner.listen: Listen to his recording of Pictures at an Exhibition with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra and notice how precisely the orchestral groups come in together. Try to hear how clearly the different instruments stay distinct from one another.

artiest/froukje.text:
Froukje Veenstra was born in 2001 in Nieuwkoop. She went to school in Alphen aan den Rijn and at sixteen moved to Rotterdam to study at Codarts, the conservatoire. She belongs to the generation that around 2020 first found an audience through social media and streaming, and only afterwards through radio and a record company.

Her first song, Groter dan ik, appeared in early 2020. It began as a study assignment at the conservatoire and became a protest song about the climate crisis. Within a year it had been streamed 1.7 million times. Later that year came Ik wil dansen, her first song in the Single Top 100. In 2021 that title became a slogan at protests for the reopening of nightlife, when clubs were closed because of the coronavirus measures. Froukje writes her music with a laptop, a guitar or a keyboard, and makes synth-pop: electronic sounds with clear, personal lyrics. The EP Licht en donker (January 2021) reached second place in the album chart.

After the EP Uitzinnig (2022), her first album, Noodzakelijk verdriet, appeared in January 2024. It reached number 1 in the Netherlands and Flanders and won an Edison for best album in 2025. She also collaborated with the rapper S10. Froukje follows an old line in Dutch-language pop. Boudewijn de Groot sang a protest song about the Vietnam War in 1966. She sings in her own language about the future of the planet, for an audience her own age.
artiest/froukje.listen: Groter dan ik began as a study assignment. Listen to the lyrics: Froukje sings in the first person about the feeling that the climate crisis is too big for one person. Set it beside Welterusten mijnheer de president by Boudewijn de Groot: the same kind of protest, but personal rather than addressed to a person in power.

artiest/fumio-hayasaka.text: Fumio Hayasaka (1914–1955) was largely self-taught. From Yoidore tenshi (1948) he was Akira Kurosawa's regular composer. For Rashōmon (1950) Kurosawa asked him for music in the spirit of Ravel's Boléro: a constantly repeated rhythm above which the melody slowly swells. Hayasaka blended Western orchestral music with elements from the Japanese tradition, such as Noh and gagaku. For Kenji Mizoguchi he wrote Ugetsu monogatari (1953), among others. In Shichinin no samurai (1954) he gave the samurai and the farmers each a theme of their own. He died in 1955 of tuberculosis, while working on Kurosawa's next film. His pupil Masaru Sato completed that score.
artiest/fumio-hayasaka.listen: In the Rashōmon suite, listen to how a single rhythmic pattern keeps going while the instrumentation expands, as in Ravel's Boléro.

artiest/funkadelic.text:
Funkadelic began as the backing band of The Parliaments, the doo-wop group of George Clinton from Plainfield, New Jersey. In 1967 Clinton brought in the bassist Billy Bass Nelson and the guitarist Eddie Hazel, and soon afterwards the guitarist Tawl Ross and the drummer Tiki Fulwood. When Clinton was no longer allowed to use the name The Parliaments because of a dispute with a record label, the group carried on from 1968 as Funkadelic. The band moved to Detroit and signed with Westbound.

The first albums, Funkadelic and Free Your Mind... and Your Ass Will Follow (both 1970) and Maggot Brain (1971), mixed soul and funk with hard, psychedelic rock. Jimi Hendrix, Sly Stone and the MC5 were major examples. The keyboard player Bernie Worrell became a fixture, and in 1972 Bootsy Collins and his brother Catfish joined, from James Brown's band. After the return of Parliament in 1974, almost the same musicians played in both groups. Parliament was the accessible side with vocals and horns, Funkadelic the experimental guitar band. The peak came in 1978 with One Nation Under a Groove, with a more melodic, more danceable sound. The title track spent six weeks at number 1 on the R&B chart. In 1981 the last official album appeared.

Together with Parliament, Funkadelic formed the P-Funk collective, which helped shape the funk culture of the 1970s. Many tracks from the early albums became a model for later funk, rock and hip hop artists.
artiest/funkadelic.listen: Listen to One Nation Under a Groove and notice how many voices and instruments together make one continuous groove. Hear how bass, guitar and vocals keep locking into one another, so that the song keeps rolling.

artiest/gabby-pahinui.text:
Gabby Pahinui was a Hawaiian slack-key guitarist and singer. He was born on 22 April 1921 in Lahaina on Maui, as Charles Kapono Kahahawai Jr., in a poor family that sold leis. Later he was informally adopted by Emily and Philip Pahinui, from whom he took the surname. He married at seventeen and had thirteen children. He first worked as an accompanying guitarist with Charley Tiny Brown and quickly learned steel guitar, even to read music. The nickname Gabby is said to come from the gabardine trousers that were the costume for an orchestra.

Pahinui recorded in the 1960s and 1970s, including Hawaiian Slack Key Guitar Instrumental Vol. II in 1962, Gabby in 1972 and Pure Gabby in 1978. He also became known as Pops Pahinui and died on 13 October 1980. His son Cyril Pahinui carried the tradition on. Hi'ilawe from 1978 is on Pure Gabby.

Slack key is a Hawaiian way of playing the guitar, in which the strings are loosened to an open tuning. The thumb plays a continuous bass line while the fingers play the melody, so that one guitar sounds like a small band. Pahinui also sang in Hawaiian, with a warm, relaxed voice. He is seen as one of the most important voices of Hawaiian music and as a source of inspiration for later generations of guitarists and singers from the islands.
artiest/gabby-pahinui.listen: Listen to Hi'ilawe and notice how the thumb plays a calm bass line while the fingers lay the melody on top of it. Does it sound as if more than one guitarist is playing?

artiest/gabriel-yared.text: Gabriel Yared was born in 1949 in Beirut and settled in Paris in the 1970s. There he first worked as an arranger for French pop singers. He wrote his first film music for Jean-Luc Godard's Sauve qui peut (la vie) (1980). In 37°2 le matin (1986) he mixed piano, saxophone and light electronics. He broke through internationally with L'amant (1992) and above all The English Patient (1996). That score, with strings, piano and Hungarian folk singing, won an Oscar. For Das Leben der Anderen (2006) he wrote, with Stéphane Moucha, the piano sonata that makes the Stasi officer in the film change his mind.
artiest/gabriel-yared.listen: Notice the intimate piano lines and the warm strings, and how a single melody returns in different line-ups.

artiest/gabrieli-consort-en-players.text:
The Gabrieli Consort & Players is a British early music ensemble, consisting of a choir and an orchestra that plays on period instruments. The ensemble was founded in 1982 by the conductor Paul McCreesh. The name refers to Giovanni Gabrieli, the Venetian composer and organist who worked at the Basilica di San Marco around 1600 and became famous for his music for multiple choirs and instrumental groups.

That Venetian repertoire is central to the ensemble's recordings. A Venetian Coronation 1595 appeared in 1990 and brings together music from the Venetian tradition. Music for San Rocco from 1996 and Venetian Easter Mass from 1997 follow on from it. The group also recorded Palestrina Mass: Hodie Christus natus est in 1993, Requiem Officium Defunctorum, 1605 in 1995 and Handel's Messiah in 1997. Earlier, in 1987, the oratorios Jephthah, The Judgement of Solomon and Jonah appeared.

The Gabrieli Consort & Players belongs to the movement that wants early music to sound as it was originally conceived, with small, agile line-ups and instruments of the period.
artiest/gabrieli-consort-en-players.listen: Listen to a piece from A Venetian Coronation 1595 and notice how different groups of singers and instruments alternate. Try to hear how large the space sounds in which that music was meant to be heard.
